display_title: Aspirin after PCI in Acute Coronary Syndromes
summary: A letter by Li, Zhang and Liu argues that the timing of aspirin withdrawal deserves further study after PCI; it provides no new randomized comparison or validated treatment rule.
research_question: Does the timing of aspirin withdrawal help frame interpretation of early ischemic risk in NEO-MINDSET, and what should future de-escalation studies examine?
author_summary: Li, Zhang and Liu interpret the NEO-MINDSET result through the timing of aspirin withdrawal. They highlight that 83% of monotherapy patients who had stent thrombosis experienced it within 30 days, as reported in their letter, and propose studying time-adaptive de-escalation and platelet-function testing. This is commentary on prior evidence, not a new trial or proof that testing-guided withdrawal improves outcomes. Only their signed letter is synthesized; the other letters and trialists' reply sharing this DOI are excluded.

study_profile.evidence_type: Interpretation of prior trial evidence and a research proposal
study_profile.translation_scope: Hypothesis and trial-design discussion; not individualized antiplatelet advice
study_profile.counting_note: The 83% figure describes when thrombosis occurred among monotherapy patients who had stent thrombosis, not the risk among all monotherapy patients. The authors do not introduce a new patient cohort.

key_findings.claim: The authors frame early aspirin withdrawal as a timing question in interpreting the NEO-MINDSET result.
key_findings.context: Their interpretation of an existing trial; no new randomization or causal test of withdrawal timing.
key_findings.source_locator: NEJM 394(10), pp. 1035-1036; Li, Zhang and Liu letter, opening sentence and continuation across the page break; PMID 41780015.

key_findings.claim: The letter highlights an early concentration of stent thrombosis among affected monotherapy patients.
key_findings.context: Among monotherapy patients who experienced stent thrombosis, the letter reports that it occurred in 83% within 30 days; this is not an 83% event rate in the entire treatment group.

evidence.label: affected monotherapy patients whose thrombosis occurred within the early interval

key_findings.source_locator: NEJM 394(10), p. 1036; Li, Zhang and Liu letter, sentence reporting stent-thrombosis timing immediately after the page-break continuation.

key_findings.claim: The authors propose future studies of time-adaptive de-escalation, including platelet-function testing.
key_findings.context: A proposed way to study changing thrombosis and bleeding risks, without a tested decision threshold or demonstrated outcome benefit.

evidence.label: proposed investigation
evidence.value: Time-adaptive de-escalation with pharmacodynamic platelet-function testing

key_findings.source_locator: NEJM 394(10), p. 1036; final sentence of the Li, Zhang and Liu letter, before their three-author signature.

what_this_adds: A specific timing-based interpretation of an existing antiplatelet trial.
A research proposal for studying adaptive transitions rather than a proven treatment algorithm.

supports: Attribution of the timing argument and proposed research agenda to Li, Zhang and Liu.
Accurate reporting of the letter's early-event proportion with its restricted denominator.
does_not_establish: New randomized efficacy or safety evidence.
A causal benefit of delaying aspirin withdrawal or of platelet-function-guided care.
A patient-specific stopping date or validated treatment threshold.

qa.question: Which correspondence under this shared DOI is covered?
qa.answer: Only the letter signed by Mengyao Li, Ge Zhang and Xiaozhu Liu, indexed as PMID 41780015, is covered. Other letters and the trialists' reply are excluded.

qa.question: What does the 83% figure mean?
qa.answer: Among monotherapy patients who had stent thrombosis, the letter reports that 83% experienced it within 30 days. This is not the probability of thrombosis for every monotherapy patient.

qa.question: What further investigation do the authors propose?
qa.answer: They propose studying time-adaptive de-escalation, including platelet-function testing to inform transitions as ischemic and bleeding risks evolve.

qa.question: Can this letter establish a safe aspirin-withdrawal schedule?
qa.answer: No. It supplies interpretation and a research proposal, without a new randomized comparison or validated individualized stopping rule.

limitations: The event proportion is reported by the correspondence; this synthesis does not independently reanalyze the NEO-MINDSET dataset.
The shared DOI includes separate letters and a reply. Their statistics and recommendations are not attributed to Li, Zhang and Liu.
Full text was read from the author's ResearchGate upload in an HTML text rendition; the PDF binary and a publisher-hosted full text were not retrieved.

related_papers.relationship: Related atherosclerotic plaque risk research; its observational modeling does not validate an aspirin-withdrawal strategy.

provenance.evidence_basis: The complete signed Li/Zhang/Liu letter was read in the public ResearchGate HTML rendition, with journal pagination 1035-1036. Author order, DOI and pagination match PMID 41780015; publisher issue information is March 5, 2026. Adjacent correspondence is excluded.
provenance.version: Typeset journal-version text from Meng-Yao Li's ResearchGate upload dated March 18, 2026, accessed October 26, 2026. PDF binary not retrieved; publisher-hosted full text remains restricted.
provenance.figure_verification: No figure or table occurs in the reviewed signed letter; no image is reproduced.

evidence_page_notice: This page interprets the Li, Zhang and Liu letter (PMID 41780015), not all correspondence sharing the DOI. It reports no new clinical experiment and does not establish an aspirin-withdrawal schedule.
